title: GOLD: Public inquiry needed after IIU cover-up in Bradley Singer shooting
article: Why did delivering Bradley Singer's mental health warrant turn into an execution last year? The Internal Investigation Unit, mandated to investigate police shootings, refused to answer that question.

The police watchdog knew how fishy their final report on the Singer killing was. That's why they released it out the back door, late on a Friday in January when reporters are likely to have gone home for the weekend and too late for anyone to follow up with questions.
The tactic was successful, as not a single reporter has asked a single question of the IIU about the report, simply regurgitating what it says.
However, as we say at the new Winnipeg Sun: Facts matter.
A Mental Health Order is NOT a death warrant. The IIU report about the Singer killing demonstrates to what end the IIU will go to exonerate police, and that's why a public inquiry is needed.

It wasn't the first time cops had stormed Singer's home on Magnus Avenue to take him to a doctor. In Jan. 2024, they caused thousands of dollars in damage while apprehending Singer to take him to an appointment.
A few weeks later, after his mental health worker attested Singer was off his medication and had not been attending appointments, two officers showed up before dawn knocking at the side door.

The 59-year-old opened the door, saw it was police, and closed it. As the cops called for back-up, Singer opened the door again, pounded a crowbar on the door frame, said "you know what this is for," and shut the door.
Why did they show up before sunrise?

Right after the killing, a press release explained, "On Feb. 8, 2024, the Winnipeg Police Service received an order under the Manitoba Mental Health Act... to convey him to hospital for a non-voluntary physician examination. Officers made several attempts during the following days to apprehend the male but were met with negative results."

One officer already had his gun out when Singer, who they knew was mentally unwell, sprayed a fire extinguisher at them when they began to pry the doorframe. In response, more and more officers came to the house, 16 in total, with fatal results.

The IIU wasn't interested in why the police were in such a hurry to apprehend Singer, but it's an important detail. The order had a 7 day limit. Police were trying to haul Singer in before it expired. Otherwise, they'd have to explain to the court how Winnipeg's finest were stymied and ask for another warrant.

After smashing into the house, nine gun-toting TST members, each wearing 17 pounds of body armour, went up the stairs where Singer was behind a bedroom door. An officer tried the door and Singer came out "aggressively."
The IIU spoke with the officer in command, WO4, about what happened next.

He observed one of the officers who shot Singer (SO2), and another cop with a beanbag gun "moving suddenly backward on the landing and into the wall beside the stairs, [and I] thought the officers were possibly being pushed down the stairs."
He then "observed SO2 bringing up his rifle and firing three or four times." Due to the angle of the stairs at the landing, he could not see the other shooter or Singer.

The second-in-command, WO5, told the IIU: "[Singer] had a wooden object in his hands and appeared to be pushing it in a horizontal fashion towards the ballistic shield and officers. The three officers moved suddenly backwards into the wall of the staircase/landing. At the same moment, [I] heard gunshots and observed SO2 discharge his gun."

What the senior officers described was basically a hockey cross-check. However, the two officers who fired the shots claimed Singer was swinging an axe, and struck a police shield before he was immediately gunned down.
They refused to speak with the investigation directly, providing carefully lawyered statements. Those cops could not be questioned about their version of events.

The IIU determined that it wasn't necessary to count the number of stairs, the number of shots fired, or corroborate their claims Singer was swinging an axe. The wounds on his arms certainly don't seem to corroborate it.
Acting Civilian Director, Bruce Sychuk, instead contorted himself to justify the shooting. Everybody else's accounts were dismissed.
Sychuk also didn't compare how the police service managed other stand-offs in the month before Singer was massacred under the guise of, "we're here to help you."

Three days prior, a six hour stand-off on College Avenue took place after two men fired a shotgun and three policemen were hit by pellets. Two weeks before that, a standoff in Transcona lasted three hours after a report of a woman being held by a man with a gun. In both cases, a crisis negotiator came to the scene and no one was shot by police.

The day of the killing, "These IIU people come to my residence and tell me that Brad was involved in what they called: An altercation with police officers and he's been shot several times," said Bradley's brother Gerry.
"They left this huge puddle of his blood there in the house... I'm not sure he made it to the hospital alive," Gerry explained. "They wouldn't let us see his body one last time. Why?"
The IIU was not interested in peaceful ways the incident could have been ended, with Singer alive. "I learned as it went along, their investigation was to justify the gun fight."
When the IIU Civilian Director met with the family weeks ago, "he seemed to be troubled by the words he was speaking," said Gerry.
"He couldn't look us in the eye... he didn't even give us a copy of the report. I thought they were going to give us something. They didn't give us the officer's names."
"I couldn't believe they shot him dead executing a mental health warrant," said Gerry. "It's so unnecessary for this to happen."
Gerry agrees a public inquiry would be able to probe just what was necessary, and call all the police and doctors involved to testify.
The other standoffs lasted for hours. The police had all the time in the world to get the help and advice of a mental health professional.
The Mental Health Act contains an important definition: Reasonable measures.
12(2) A peace officer may take any reasonable measures when acting under this section or section 9 or 11 or subsection 44(1) or 48(2)...

The IIU would define "reasonable measures" as what happened to Bradley Singer. Under this precedent, police acting under the umbrella of the Manitoba Mental Health Act are untouchable. They cannot be charged or even disciplined internally for anything they do in the course of serving a Mental Health Order.
"I find it very telling that nobody from the police have said "we're sorry this happened."
This wasn't a crime in progress. If the Winnipeg police are called out to help someone and wind up killing him, then they have failed in their job.
Should parents and friends of mentally ill people in distress call police? Or are they condemning their children and friends to death.
A public inquiry is needed to answer these questions. And maybe, to determine if the biased IIU should be disbanded.
